extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy of science, foundations of mathematics, and epistemology
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and philosophical standards for judging the nature, origin, and legitimacy of first principles (axioms and definitions) and scientific hypotheses, especially in geometry and physical science. Focuses on whether such principles are empirical, hypothetical, or a priori, and what evidence justifies them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypotheses must relate to real existence
rubrics_metrics.description: An hypothesis framed for scientific inquiry must relate to something which has real existence (for there can be no science respecting nonentities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: We must not ascribe to the thing any property which it has not; our liberty extends only to slightly exaggerating some of those which it has (by assuming it to be completely what it really is very nearly), and suppressing others, under the indispensable obligation of restoring them whenever, and in as far as, their presence or absence would make any material difference in the truth of our conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible idealization: slight exaggeration or suppression
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypotheses may slightly exaggerate or suppress some properties of a real object to facilitate study, provided such changes are not 'distinctly false' or 'repugnant to its real nature.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Idealizations that merely divest a real object of some portion of its properties (without clothing it in false ones) yield conclusions that, with known liabilities to correction, will express actual truth. But arbitrary hypotheses about non-existent objects may be intellectually useful for illustration without adding to knowledge of nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish definitions (hypothetical first principles) from axioms
rubrics_metrics.description: Some first principles involved in definitions are hypothetical (adopted for illustration) while axioms are fundamental truths that must be admitted among first principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although certain axioms can be rephrased as definitions or proved by imaginary superposition, there remain fundamental axioms (e.g., 'two straight lines cannot inclose a space') that are indemonstrable and not merely definitional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axioms are true without mixture of hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Axioms differ from definitional first principles because they are true without any mixture of hypothesis; they hold of real lines and figures just as of imaginary ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This makes mathematics similar to other sciences where some general propositions are exactly true (e.g., first law of motion) while many others are approximations that may be feigned as exact for practical use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence for axioms: experimental generalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Axioms rest on experimental truths; they are generalizations from observation rather than purely a priori intuitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Two straight lines cannot inclose a space' is treated as an induction from the evidence of our senses — repeated observation confirms it to an extent surpassing many ordinary physical truths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for a priori claim: chronological independence from experience
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish that an axiom is known a priori, one must show chronologically that the conviction arises prior to the relevant sensory impressions (i.e., prior to the experiences on which the experiential account would base belief).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This point is often unprovable because such early cognitive states are beyond memory and direct external observation; failure to prove chronological independence weakens the a priori claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental intuition (imaginary looking) only counts if mental images replicate experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Perceiving a geometrical truth by 'merely thinking of' straight lines is epistemically valid only because our mental images of form have exactness comparable to sensory impressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imagination-based 'experiments' are legitimate when prior experience has taught us that images faithfully represent real objects; otherwise mental inspection would not reliably substitute for observation. This also answers the objection about inability to observe lines 'to infinity' — mental extension is acceptable if imagery is trustworthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquisition of concepts supplies experiential evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The psychological process of acquiring the idea (e.g., of straightness or whole/part) involves concrete experience sufficient to verify the associated axiomatic proposition when the terms are understood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As Bain's argument: 'When we have mastered the notion of straightness, we have also mastered that aspect ... that two straight lines cannot inclose a space.' Thus apparent intuition often packs prior observational learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inconceivability is not a reliable indicator of necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: The fact that the negation of a proposition is 'inconceivable' for us does not prove it to be necessarily true in itself, because inconceivableness heavily depends on habitual associations and past experiences of the mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples (e.g., antipodes, gravitational theory, acceptance of Newtonian physics) show that what was once deemed inconceivable later became conceivable; thus using inconceivability as proof of a priori necessity is fallible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological transformation: experimental truths can appear necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Propositions discovered empirically (e.g., laws of motion, chemical composition) may, after becoming familiar, be felt as self-evident or necessary though originally grounded in experiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This illustrates that the feeling of necessity can be a psychological effect of repeated confirmation and association rather than evidence of an a priori foundation; an evaluator must account for this process before labeling a truth as necessary in a metaphysical sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity requires ruling out associative origins
rubrics_metrics.description: To claim a proposition is necessarily true (not merely empirically well-confirmed), one must show that its apparent necessity is not the product of association or the history of mental habit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since habitual association can make an experimental conviction seem inconceivable in the contrary, proponents of genuine necessity bear the burden of demonstrating that associative psychology does not explain the conviction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose-sensitive acceptability of arbitrary hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: When the purpose is mere illustration or intellectual exercise, arbitrary hypotheses (about imaginary animals or commonwealths) are acceptable though they do not increase knowledge of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish aims: use arbitrary hypotheses for demonstration or training, but do not mistake their conclusions for empirical truths about real objects; only hypotheses tied to real existence can inform science.
